parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The magnitude of the gravitational potential on the surface of a planet of radius *R* is *φ*. The planet can be considered to be an isolated sphere.

On Fig. 2.1, sketch the variation of the gravitational potential with distance *x* from the centre of the planet for values of *x* between *R* and 4*R*.

[[fig:f1]]

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A satellite is in a geostationary orbit above the Earth. At time *t* = 0, the magnitude of the gravitational potential due to the Earth at the location of the satellite is *φ*.

On Fig. 2.2, sketch the variation of the gravitational potential due to the Earth at the location of the satellite for values of *t* between *t* = 0 and *t* = 24 hours.

[[fig:f2]]

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
The electric potential difference (p.d.) between two parallel plates is *V*, as shown in Fig. 2.3.

[[fig:f3]]

The distance between the plates is *d*. The region between the plates is a vacuum.

On Fig. 2.4, sketch the variation of the electric potential with distance from the positive plate.

[[fig:f4]]

figures.alt: A blank graph grid for gravitational potential against distance x, with the vertical axis marked from −φ to φ and the horizontal axis marked from 0 to 4R.

figures.caption: Fig. 2.2
figures.alt: A blank graph grid for gravitational potential against time, with the vertical axis marked from −2φ to 2φ and the horizontal axis marked from 0 to 24 hours.

figures.caption: Fig. 2.3
figures.alt: Two horizontal parallel plates are separated by distance d, with a potential difference V, a positive terminal connected to the upper plate and the lower plate earthed.
